name: Tax Justice Network (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by income group: revenue in low and lower-middle income countries 85% (India, the largest lower-middle income country in the Global Forum's revenue figures, 30%; the rest equally over the nine African countries whose tax authorities the network works with in its 2025 report: Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Uganda, Ethiopia, Zambia, Tanzania, Rwanda and Benin), upper-middle income 13% (Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, South Africa), high income 1% (the UK as a stand-in). A judgment: no country split of the revenue is published.
summary: The Tax Justice Network, a UK non-profit research and advocacy company founded in 2003 (GBP 2.09 million spent in 2025), proposed the tax-transparency standards now in force worldwide (automatic exchange of tax information, ownership registers, country-by-country reporting) and campaigns for the UN tax convention due in 2027. An average year of its spending since 2003 is counted against its judged 1.8% share of five years of the revenue those standards raise (the OECD Global Forum's EUR 4 billion a year, 70% in developing countries) and 3% of a 40% chance that the convention recovers a twentieth of the US$47 billion lower-income countries lose each year; revenue in low and lower-middle income countries is valued as GiveWell values government spending (about 1.5 times cash), elsewhere as money spread over citizens' consumption, both net of what it costs the rich who pay. With the next dollar at 54% of the average, it comes to about 2 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, more than ten times its peers because the work is valued through public revenue for lower-income governments, a large sum worth more per dollar than the outcomes most advocacy models count, of which a small credited share still outweighs a budget under US$3 million a year. The result is mostly uncertainty: the network's share of the credit, the years a win counts and the share of losses the convention recovers are judgments with no study behind them, and its own ranges span over ten-thousandfold; both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: An average year of what the Tax Justice Network spent since 2003, scaled from its audited 2025 accounts (GBP 2.09 million) by a judged ratio; fundraising spread over the programme. The network is a UK non-profit company limited by guarantee, not a registered charity; donations from the US are accepted as from an equivalent of a 501(c)(3) public charity.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The public revenue the two outcomes concern: what the international transparency standards the network proposed in 2003 raise each year (the OECD Global Forum's count, split by income group), and what countries lose each year to cross-border tax abuse, the UN tax convention's target.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What a dollar of public revenue is worth: in low and lower-middle income countries GiveWell's value of a dollar of government spending, elsewhere the money spread over citizens' consumption; both less what the tax costs those who pay it. The standards count the years a won reform counts; the convention is a chance, after a wait.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's share of the credit (the network's share of the movement's resources, times civil society's share of all), trust in the figures, the share collected or applied, missing data and side effects; the canonical rows are their outcome-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Both branches' credited value, spread over the 23 years of work since 2003, per dollar of an average year's spending.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Consumption per person of those who pay the tax, as a multiple of the UK average
rows.explainer: Offshore wealth and shifted profits belong mostly to the richest households: Alstadsaeter, Johannesen and Zucman (2019) find the top 0.01% own about half of the offshore wealth in Scandinavian leaks, and shareholders of multinationals are mostly rich households and pension funds in rich countries. rows.explainer: Domestic money's rule (docs/normalization.md 2.20): the recipients' gain less the payers' cost; a dollar taken from someone consuming c costs 1/c in ln(consumption), valued at the shared rate.

rows.label: UN convention: share of countries' yearly losses it recovers once in force
rows.explainer: The framework convention's terms cover fair allocation of taxing rights, taxing high-net-worth individuals, illicit financial flows and dispute resolution, through a framework text and early protocols (taxation of cross-border services; disputes). Its own text is due in 2027, the protocols' content and the countries that ratify them uncertain; no comparable reform has a measured effect to anchor on. Judged 5% of lower-income countries' losses (1% to 20%), if it comes into force with substance.

source.quote: the collective, worldwide funding from philanthropy and bilateral government donors in the six years to 2025 was less than US$10 million a year

rows.explainer: Coalition credit by resources (Convention 2). The funders' group TAIC tracks under US$10 million a year of philanthropic and bilateral funding to tax justice, of which the network's own (about US$2.5 million a year, mostly from Norad, the Open Society Foundations and the FCDO) is a quarter; but large NGOs (Oxfam, ActionAid, Christian Aid, Eurodad, the Global Alliance for Tax Justice, the FACT Coalition, Global Witness and Transparency International on beneficial ownership) spend their own unrestricted money on it too, and did more so in the 2010s. Judged 12% (5% to 25%).

rows.label: Transparency standards: civil society's share of the resources behind them
rows.explainer: Governments did most: the G20's 2009 push after the financial crisis, the US FATCA law (2010), which made automatic exchange workable, the OECD secretariat and the Global Forum's peer reviews, the EU's directives, and the leaks journalists published (LuxLeaks, the Panama Papers). Civil society proposed the measures first and kept them on the agenda. Judged 15% (5% to 35%).

rows.label: Transparency standards: the network's share of the credit
rows.explainer: Its share of civil society's resources times civil society's share of all.

rows.label: Transparency standards: trust in the revenue figure
rows.explainer: The revenue is what tax authorities report having identified, not an evaluation; some would have been found by other means. Judged 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), as for Transparency International's policy branch's trust in its changes (0.5) but higher, as the revenue is counted.

rows.label: Transparency standards: share that wouldn't have happened anyway

rows.label: Transparency standards: share of the identified revenue collected
rows.explainer: Identified revenue includes assessments still under appeal or never paid; voluntary disclosures are mostly paid. Judged 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: Transparency standards: discount for missing data

source.quote: a statistically significant 22% reduction in IFC bank deposits

rows.explainer: The Global Forum counts revenue found in investigations and disclosure programmes, not the income people now declare because their accounts are reported: the start of automatic exchange is linked to a 22% fall in the deposits that residents of other countries hold in financial centres, exchange on request to about 10%. Judged half as much again (10% to 200%).

source.quote: Country by country reporting, a basic transparency measure that we and other like-minded stakeholders have been championing since 2003

rows.explainer: Tax authorities use multinationals' country-by-country reports to pick audits, and ownership registers serve anti-money-laundering and corruption cases as well as tax; little of this is in the Global Forum's figure, and no total is published. Judged 10% (0 to 50%).

rows.label: Side effect: banks' and firms' cost of reporting, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Financial institutions spend heavily on reporting under the Common Reporting Standard, but the cost falls on firms and customers in rich countries, worth little on the log scale against revenue for lower-income governments. Judged -2% (-10% to 0).

source.quote: a process which reflects the leadership of the African Group of countries and the decades-long work of the international tax justice movement

rows.explainer: Governments lead: the African Group's resolutions (2022, 2023), the UN's negotiating committee and its secretariat; civil society proposed a UN tax body for two decades and supplies analysis, statements and coordination. rows.label: UN convention: trust in the losses it addresses
rows.explainer: The losses are the network's own estimate, from methods others contest (the OECD's and the IMF's estimates of profit shifting differ by a factor of two either way); the convention's effect is in b_share_recovered. Judged 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9).

rows.label: UN convention: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years counted already say it would have come some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: UN convention: share applied as agreed
rows.explainer: Tax authorities in lower-income countries apply new treaty rights slowly and partly (the Addis Tax Initiative's reports of thin audit capacity). Judged 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: UN convention: discount for missing data
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no evaluation of the network's part, and no outcome yet; the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: UN convention: total adjustment

rows.explainer: The US is the one country not negotiating (2025 report p. 4) and opposes taxes on its multinationals; the network's own report notes the 2025 G7 exemption of US multinationals from the global minimum tax. Some of the convention's gains may be offset. Judged -5% (-20% to 0).
